opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think visual intelligence is really the missing piece between where we are with language models and where we want to be with general-purpose robots.

Language models have been extraordinarily successful, partly because language is a compressed, human-curated representation of the world. Someone has already done the hard work of abstracting reality into symbols, so the model learns from that distilled signal. But a robot doesn't live in that distilled world. It lives in the raw, continuous, messy physical world, where you have to perceive geometry, objects, materials, motion, cause and effect, and you have to do it in real time.

So I often say that language is a kind of shortcut. It gets you surprisingly far on reasoning and knowledge, but it doesn't give you grounding. If you only learn from text, you know that a cup can fall off a table, but you don't really have an internal model of how it falls, how fast, where it lands, or what happens if your hand is slightly off. For robotics, that grounding is the whole game.

That's why I think vision has to move from being a "perception module" that feeds labels into a language model, to being a foundation in its own right. Right now, many multimodal systems treat vision as a front end: encode the image, turn it into tokens, and let the language model do the thinking. That's useful, but it's backwards for embodied intelligence. Humans and animals developed rich visual and spatial understanding long before language. A lot of intelligence, like spatial reasoning, intuitive physics, and planning your movements, happens without words.

I see a few things as central. First, spatial intelligence: understanding 3D structure, where things are relative to each other and to you, not just what category they belong to. Second, world models: being able to predict how a scene evolves, especially in response to your own actions. That's essentially imagination, and it's what lets an agent plan rather than just react. Third, learning from video at scale. Video is the closest thing we have to the internet-scale data that powered language models, but for the physical world. Figuring out how to extract good representations from it, without relying entirely on language supervision, is still an open and very important problem.

I'd also say there's a healthy tension in the field right now. One camp thinks we can scale vision-language-action models and language will remain the backbone. I think that will produce useful systems, but I'm skeptical it leads to truly general robots by itself. The data bottleneck for robotics is real, and the way to address it is probably to build strong visual world understanding first, from passive observation, and then connect it to action with relatively less robot data, much like a child watches the world for a long time before acting skillfully in it.

So in short, language models gave us a proof that scaling and general-purpose learning work. Visual intelligence is what will let that generality actually touch the physical world. I think the next few years will be less about making models talk better and more about making them see, understand space, and imagine consequences. That's the path toward robots that are genuinely general.

r002.rationale: It defines world models as predicting how a scene evolves, especially in response to the agent’s own actions.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention coding agents as an interface for language models to affect the physical world.

r004.rationale: It frames visual intelligence as the missing bridge between language models and general-purpose robotics, then describes spatial understanding, world models, and video learning as parts of that path.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think this question gets at something I've been thinking about for a long time, and my honest view is that vision is not just one more modality we bolt onto a language model. It's closer to the foundation that general-purpose robotics actually has to be built on.

Here's how I'd frame it. Language models succeeded because the internet gave us an enormous corpus of human thought already compressed into symbols. Text is a very efficient carrier of abstract knowledge. But the physical world doesn't come pre-tokenized. A robot has to deal with continuous geometry, lighting, occlusion, object permanence, the fact that a cup looks different from every angle but is still the same cup. None of that is written down anywhere in a form you can just read. You have to perceive it.

So when people say "we'll take a strong LLM and add a vision encoder and then connect it to actions," I think that underestimates the problem. In our own work on multimodal models, what we kept finding was that the visual representations were the bottleneck, not the language side. The language model was very good at reasoning once it had the right information, but the vision encoder often didn't give it the right information. It would miss spatial relationships, counting, fine-grained details, depth. These are exactly the things a robot needs to get right every single time, not most of the time.

The other point I'd make is about what "visual intelligence" even means. I don't think it's just recognition. Recognition is the part we solved first because it's closest to classification, which is what we knew how to do. The harder and more important piece is something like visual world modeling, the ability to look at a scene and understand what's possible in it. What will happen if I push this? What's behind that? Where can I put my hand? That's spatial and physical reasoning grounded in perception, and I think that's what separates a model that can describe a kitchen from one that can work in a kitchen.

And then there's the data question, which is really the crux for robotics. We don't have an internet of robot trajectories. We're not going to get one at the scale we got text. So the question becomes, where does the general knowledge come from? My bet is that a lot of it has to come from video and from vision more broadly, because that's the one place where we have massive, diverse, cheap data about how the physical world actually behaves. If you can learn a strong visual representation of the world from passive observation, then the robot-specific data only needs to teach the mapping from that understanding to action. That's a much smaller problem than learning everything from scratch through interaction.

I'd also be a bit careful about the word "general-purpose." I think we sometimes let the success of LLMs make us believe generality comes for free from scale. In vision and robotics, I think generality is going to come from the right representations and the right objectives, and scale amplifies those but doesn't replace them. If the representation doesn't capture 3D structure, scaling it won't give you 3D structure.

So to answer your question directly: I see visual intelligence as the thing that connects the abstract knowledge in language models to the concrete, messy reality that robots have to operate in. Language gives you the "what" and the "why." Vision has to give you the "where" and the "how." And right now the second part is much less mature than the first, which is exactly why I think it's the most interesting place to be working.

r003.rationale: It does not identify coding agents as an interface for language models to affect the physical world.

astra-6.text:
I think visual intelligence is central, because a robot has to connect what it knows to what is actually happening around it. A language model might describe how to pick up a cup, but the robot still needs to locate the cup, understand its shape, decide where to grasp it, and notice whether it’s slipping. Those are problems of perception coupled with action.

And vision here means more than recognizing objects. It means understanding space, motion, and how the world changes when you interact with it. If I push something, what will happen? If an object disappears behind another object, is it still there? The system needs an understanding that supports those predictions.

Language can provide a very powerful interface for goals and knowledge. But for general-purpose robotics, that has to connect to a continuous loop: observe, act, and update your understanding based on the result. A plan that sounds reasonable can fail immediately in the physical world.

So I see visual intelligence as a core part of that loop. The challenge is learning representations that are useful for doing things, and that remain useful when the robot encounters an unfamiliar object or environment. That’s where the connection between perception, learning, and control becomes especially important.

sol-6.1.text:
I think visual intelligence is central because a robot has to connect what it knows to what is actually happening around it. Language gives you a powerful way to represent goals and communicate knowledge, but it doesn’t automatically tell you where an object is, how it moves, or what will happen when you touch it.

Imagine asking a robot to clear a table. The instruction is simple. But the robot has to recognize unfamiliar objects, understand which ones are fragile, see that one object is partly hidden behind another, and keep updating its understanding as it acts. That requires perception tied closely to action.

So I wouldn’t describe this as simply moving from language models to robots by adding a camera. The deeper challenge is learning representations that connect vision, language, and physical experience. Can the system predict the consequences of an action? Can it recognize when its prediction was wrong and recover?

To me, that feedback loop is essential for general-purpose robotics. A robot needs to learn from the world continuously, and vision is a major part of how it gets that feedback.
